title: Missing Plot Technique in Block Designs
breadcrumb: Unit III · Design of Experiments · Missing observations
objectives: Explain why missing plot values complicate block-design analysis.
Apply the one-missing-value estimator in a randomised block design.
Apply the one-missing-value estimator in a Latin square design.
Recalculate sums of squares and adjust error degrees of freedom after estimation.
Recognise limitations of simple missing-value formulas and the need for iterative methods with multiple omissions.

traps: In the RBD formula, t is number of treatments and r is number of blocks/replications; do not swap them.
Use treatment, block and grand totals calculated without the missing observation.

howto: Locate the missing cell and identify the design. For one RBD omission use x=(tB+rT−G)/((t−1)(r−1)); for one Latin-square omission use x=[p(R+C+T)−2G]/[(p−1)(p−2)]. All totals exclude the missing cell. Substitute x, recompute the ANOVA components and reduce error df by one.

scenes.title: Why a plot value may be missing
scenes.objective: Understand missing observations in designed experiments.
body: An experimental unit may be lost because of crop failure, equipment damage, sample destruction or recording error. The resulting missing cell disrupts the balance of the original design.
Classical missing plot techniques estimate a value under the design model so that the ANOVA can be completed with an adjustment. The estimate is not a recovered measurement.

items.ask: Why does a missing plot matter in a balanced block design?
items.recall: It breaks the complete treatment-by-block layout and affects sums of squares.
refresh: The original design expects a value in every planned cell.
The missing cell changes treatment and block totals.

A classical estimate allows a model-based ANOVA completion.  This rebuild makes the prerequisite explicit before the new design method is used. Identify what is being counted, which units are independent, and which assumptions allow the calculation. Then explain how that idea supports the next step rather than memorising the symbol alone.

items.recall: The sum of observed responses assigned to one treatment.
refresh: In a complete block design each treatment appears once in every block.
If one response is missing, calculate the treatment total from the observed cells only.
The same exclusion applies to the affected block total and grand total in the RBD estimator.
Do not insert a guessed value before solving for the missing observation.

items.ask: What is an error degree of freedom?
items.recall: The number of independent residual contrasts remaining after fitting the design model.
refresh: Degrees of freedom count independent pieces of information, not just the number of rows in a table.
Estimating an additional parameter uses information that would otherwise contribute to residual variation.
For one classically estimated missing plot, reduce the error degrees of freedom by one.
The estimate completes the ANOVA but is not an independently observed replicate.

scenes.title: Locate the missing cell and identify the design
scenes.objective: Distinguish RBD and Latin square omissions.
body: First identify the layout. In a randomised block design, each block contains every treatment. In a Latin square, each treatment occurs once in every row and column.
The formula depends on the layout and the totals surrounding the missing cell. Never choose a formula before identifying the design.

scenario.teaser: One crop plot is lost in a complete RBD.
scenario.title: Identify the required totals
body: The missing observation lies in treatment i and block j. Let t be the number of treatments and r the number of blocks. Let B be the affected block total, T the affected treatment total and G the grand total, each excluding the missing value.
The RBD estimator combines these totals with the design dimensions.

The estimator is derived for a particular layout and uses only observed totals. Once the value is estimated, the completed table supports recalculation of the design sums of squares, but the estimate does not become a new independent observation. State the design, define each total, and apply the degrees-of-freedom adjustment explicitly.
scenario.q: Which two totals correspond to the missing cell's row and column in an RBD?
scenario.answer: Its treatment total T and its block total B.

ask.q: What should you identify before selecting a missing-value formula?

scenes.title: RBD estimator for one missing value
scenes.objective: State and interpret the RBD formula.

blocks.body: x̂=(tB+rT−G)/[(t−1)(r−1)]. Here t is the number of treatments and r the number of blocks.
B is the affected block total, T is the affected treatment total and G is the grand total, all calculated without the missing observation.
This is the classical single-missing-value estimator for a balanced RBD under its usual additive model assumptions.

ask.q: In the RBD formula, what does t represent?
ask.nudge: Count the treatments, not the blocks.

scenes.title: Latin square estimator
scenes.objective: State and interpret the Latin-square formula.

blocks.body: x̂=[p(R+C+T)−2G]/[(p−1)(p−2)], where p is the order of the square.
R, C and T are the affected row, column and treatment totals; G is the grand total. Every total excludes the missing observation.
The Latin square has three balancing classifications—rows, columns and treatments—so its estimator differs from the RBD formula.

scenes.title: Why all totals exclude the missing value
scenes.objective: Avoid double counting the unknown cell.
body: The missing value is the unknown being estimated. If B, T, R, C or G already included a guessed value, the formula would count that value again and become circular.
Construct each required total from observed values only. Substitute the estimate only after solving the formula.

scenario.teaser: A student adds a provisional x=10 to the grand total before applying the formula.
scenario.title: Spot the double count
body: The classical formula is derived with the missing cell removed from each relevant total. Adding a guessed x to G before substitution violates that definition.
The correct procedure is to compute totals from observed entries, solve for x, then insert the estimate for the ANOVA completion.

The estimator is derived for a particular layout and uses only observed totals. Once the value is estimated, the completed table supports recalculation of the design sums of squares, but the estimate does not become a new independent observation. State the design, define each total, and apply the degrees-of-freedom adjustment explicitly.
scenario.q: Should the missing value be included in G when calculating the estimate?
scenario.answer: No. G must exclude the missing observation.

ask.q: At what stage should the estimated value be inserted into the completed table?

blocks.body: After estimating x, place it in the missing cell and recompute the relevant treatment, block, row or column totals and sums of squares according to the design.
For one estimated missing observation, reduce the error degrees of freedom by one in the classical ANOVA adjustment.

blocks.h: Do not count it as observed
blocks.body: The estimate completes the calculation but is not an independently observed replicate. Report that a missing value was estimated.

scenes.title: Multiple missing observations
scenes.objective: Recognise when simple formulas are inadequate.

blocks.body: With multiple missing values, the estimating equations may depend on one another because several row, column, treatment or block totals are incomplete.
Use the appropriate simultaneous equations or iterative procedure, updating estimates until stable under the chosen model.
Do not apply a one-missing formula separately to each omission without checking the dependency structure and design assumptions.

ask.q: Why may multiple missing values require an iterative method?
ask.nudge: The estimates can depend on each other through shared totals.

scenes.title: Choose the correct estimator
scenes.objective: Select formula by design and identify totals.
scenes.problem: A missing observation occurs in a p×p Latin square. A student proposes the RBD formula because both designs are blocked. Is that correct?
hints: Count the totals required by each formula.
Identify the design structure, apply the relevant relationship, and check the interpretation.

solution.math: A Latin square has rows, columns and treatments as three classifications.
Use x̂=[p(R+C+T)−2G]/[(p−1)(p−2)], not the RBD estimator.

scenes.check: The layout, not merely the presence of blocks, determines the formula.

scenes.intro: Mark each statement TRUE or FALSE. Read the reason after submitting all verdicts.

items.claim: The totals in the one-missing-value estimator exclude the missing observation.
items.why: Including a guessed value would double-count the unknown.

items.claim: In the RBD formula, t is the number of treatments and r is the number of blocks.
items.why: The symbols describe the two design dimensions.

items.claim: One estimated missing value reduces the classical error degrees of freedom by one.
items.why: The estimate consumes one residual degree of freedom.

items.claim: The estimated missing value is a recovered observed response.
items.why: It is a model-based estimate used to complete the analysis.

scenes.answer: RBD uses t,r,B,T,G; Latin square uses p,R,C,T,G.
